1.pericope_label: The trespass in the accursed thing and the repulse at Ai

schools.summary: Gill says the trespass was committed with respect to the accursed thing by taking part of what was devoted to another use and forbidden them, and that this was done not by the whole body of the people but by one of them; since it was not discovered who it was, it was imputed to the whole, on whom it lay. Ai he calls the next city of importance, though not so large as Jericho, three miles distant according to the Jews, four according to Abarbanel and Bunting, and he reports from Jerome that in his times very few ruins of it appeared and only the place was shown where it stood. The scouts, he says, came back to their general after reconnoitring and gave it as their opinion that there was no need for the whole army to go up; Joshua detached the largest number proposed, that there might be strength enough to take the place. Of the loss he says the thirty-six were but few, a sufficient rebuke of providence, so that their loss was small but their shame and disgrace great. Calvin says reference is made to the crime, and indeed the secret crime, of one individual whose guilt is transferred to the whole people, and that punishment is at the same time executed against several who were innocent; it seems very unaccountable that a whole people should be condemned for a private and hidden crime of which they had no knowledge. He answers that it is not new for the sin of one member to be visited on the whole body, and that should we be unable to discover the reason it ought to be more than enough for us that transgression is imputed to the children of Israel while the guilt is confined to one individual. But as it very often happens that those who are not wicked foster the sins of their brethren by conniving at them, a part of the blame is justly laid upon all those who by disguising become implicated as partners; for this reason Paul upbraids all the Corinthians with the private enormity of one individual and inveighs against their pride in presuming to glory while such a stigma attached to them. Here, however, he says it is easy to object that all were ignorant of the theft, and that therefore there is no room for the maxim that he who allows a crime to be committed when he can prevent it is its perpetrator; and he admits it is not clear why a private crime is imputed to the whole people, unless it be that they had not previously been sufficiently careful to punish misdeeds, and that possibly owing to this the person actually guilty had sinned with greater boldness, since it is well known that weeds creep in stealthily, grow apace and produce noxious fruits if not speedily torn up. Of the reconnaissance he says that to examine the site of the city and reconnoitre all its approaches was an act of prudence, that they might not by hurrying on at random through unknown places fall into an ambuscade; but that when it would be necessary shortly after to advance with all the forces, to send forward a small band with the view of taking the city seems ill advised.

Henry says the story of this chapter begins with a but: the Lord was with Joshua and his fame was noised through all that country, and it left no room to doubt that he would go on conquering and to conquer, since he did right and observed his orders in everything; but the children of Israel committed a trespass and so set God against them, and then even Joshua's name and fame, his wisdom and courage, could do them no service, for if we lose our God we lose our friends, who cannot help us unless God be for us. The sin is here only generally mentioned, being afterwards more particularly confessed from Achan's own mouth: it is the taking of the accursed thing, in disobedience to the command and in defiance of the threatening. In the sacking of Jericho orders were given that they should neither spare any lives nor take any treasure to themselves; we read not of the breach of the former prohibition, since there were none to whom they showed any mercy, but of the latter, so that compassion was put off and yielded to the law while covetousness was indulged.

Clarke's block on the first verse is an analysis of the chapter, that the trespass of the Israelites is recorded, that Joshua sends men to view the state of Ai, that they return with a favourable report, that three thousand men are sent against it and are defeated with thirty-six killed, and that Joshua is greatly distressed and prostrates himself to inquire of the Lord the reason. Ai he identifies with the place called Hai in Genesis, east of Bethel and north of Jericho, from which it was distant about ten or twelve miles, situated upon a hill and belonging to the Amorites, and very likely a strong place. The spies, he says, reported that the town was meanly garrisoned and that two or three thousand men would suffice; these were accordingly sent up and were repulsed. Of the flight he says they seem to have presumed that the men of Ai would immediately open their gates to them, and therefore marched up with confidence, but the enemy appearing they were put to flight. Wesley says the children of Israel means one of them, by a very usual figure, as that is ascribed to the disciples which belonged to Judas only, and that the accursed thing means some of the forbidden and accursed goods; Zabdi he notes is called also Zimri, and Zerah, or Zarah, was Judah's immediate son. Of the scouts' advice he says it was done by the wise contrivance of divine providence, that their sin might be punished and they awakened and reformed with as little mischief and reproach as might be. Of the flight he says they had not courage to strike a stroke, which was a plain evidence that God had forsaken them, and a useful instruction to show them what they were when God left them, and that it was God, not their own valour, that gave the Canaanites into their hands; and of the loss he calls it a dear victory to the men of Ai, whereby Israel was awakened and reformed and they hardened to their own ruin.

Keil observes that instead of Achan, the reading here and later in the book, we find Achar in Chronicles, the liquids n and r being interchanged to allow of a play upon the verb used in the twenty-fifth verse; hence in Josephus the name is spelt Acharos, and in the Vatican codex of the Septuagint Achar, whereas the Alexandrian codex has Achan. Instead of Zabdi, he adds, we find Zimri in Chronicles. Ellicott remarks that the tribe of Judah is distinguished in sacred history both for great crimes and great achievements. Why Ai should be the next town selected for attack after Jericho he calls a question which perhaps we cannot answer with certainty, observing only that the next step after its capture, before the further conquest of the country, was to set up the Ten Commandments in Mount Ebal. In the words about not making all the people labour thither he sees, by a sort of side-glance, the not unnatural comment of Israel on the seven days' march round Jericho, which they thought useless labour, being unable to appreciate the lesson it taught. The flight he calls a very natural reaction from overweening confidence to utter dismay, exhibited in the incident and in its effect, that the heart of the people melted and became as water. Shebarim he explains as the crevices or ravines, a short distance below Ai, where the road passes the head of steep glens which open into the plain of Jordan, so that the going down means until they escaped into these ravines.

debates: Why a whole people was condemned for one man's hidden crime: Calvin calls it very unaccountable, answers first that the sin of one member may be visited on the body and that connivance makes partners, then objects against himself that all were ignorant, and finally admits the reason is unclear unless they had been slack in punishing misdeeds before, while Gill and Wesley state the imputation as a usual figure without raising the difficulty

Whether the scouts advised well: Calvin allows the reconnaissance as prudence but judges it ill advised to send a small band when the whole force must shortly advance, while Wesley makes the miscarriage a contrivance of providence to punish the sin with as little mischief as might be
What the phrase about not making the people labour betrays: Ellicott alone hears in it Israel's own comment on the seven days' march round Jericho, which they thought useless labour

What the man's name was: Keil traces Achan against the Chronicler's Achar to an interchange of liquids allowing a wordplay later in the chapter, and follows the variation through Josephus and the two Greek codices
Where Ai stood and why it was attacked next: Gill and Clarke differ on the distance from Jericho, three or four miles against ten or twelve, while Ellicott declines to say why Ai was chosen at all
outliers: Calvin's admission that he cannot fully account for the imputation, and his conjecture that earlier slackness in punishing emboldened the thief
Calvin's image of weeds that creep in stealthily and produce noxious fruits if not speedily torn up
Henry's observation that the chapter begins with a but, and that if we lose our God we lose our friends
Henry's contrast that compassion yielded to the law at Jericho while covetousness was indulged
Ellicott's remark that Judah is distinguished for great crimes as well as great achievements
Ellicott's identification of Shebarim with the ravines below Ai that open into the plain of Jordan
Wesley's judgement that the small loss was a dear victory to the men of Ai, hardening them to their own ruin

6.pericope_label: Joshua rends his clothes and expostulates with God

schools.summary: Gill says the rending of the clothes was usual in those ancient times on hearing bad news, and expressive of grief and trouble. Joshua's cry he paraphrases as a lament over the miserable and distressed condition they were in, a plea for pity and compassion, and an expression of astonishment that this should have been their case; and his question what he shall say he takes as asked for the comfort and encouragement of the people of Israel, in vindication of God's power and faithfulness and against the charge of weakness in himself, unfaithfulness to his promises and unkindness to his people, brought by their enemies. The Canaanites he identifies as those that dwelt on the east and on the west of the land, one of the seven nations. Calvin says that although it was easy to throw the blame of the overthrow on others, and it was by no means becoming in a courageous leader to be so much cast down by the loss of thirty men, especially when by increasing his force a hundredfold it would not have been difficult to drive back an enemy now weary with their exertions, it was not without cause that Joshua felt the deepest sorrow and gave way to feelings bordering on despair. The thought that the events of war are doubtful, which sustains and reanimates the defeated, could not be entertained by him, because God had promised that they would always be victorious; therefore when the success did not correspond to his hopes, the only conclusion he could draw was that they had fought unsuccessfully merely because they had been deprived of the promised assistance of God. Accordingly he and the elders not only gave themselves up to sorrow but engaged in solemn mourning, as used in the most calamitous circumstances, by tearing their garments and throwing dust on their heads; that mode of expressing grief was used also by the heathen, but was specially appropriate in the pious worshippers of God in suppliantly deprecating his wrath, and the rending of the garments contained a profession of repentance, as may also be inferred from the annexed prayer. That prayer, however, is of a mixed nature, dictated partly by faith and the pure spirit of piety and partly by excessive perturbation: in turning straightway to God and acknowledging that in his hand, by which the wound was inflicted, the cure was prepared, they are influenced by faith. He adds that Joshua mentions another ground of fear, that all the neighbouring nations, who, either subdued by calamities or terrified by miracles, were quiet, would now resume their confidence and make a sudden attack upon the people, which was indeed probable.

Henry gives an account of the deep concern Joshua was in upon this sad occasion: as a public person he interested himself more than any other in the public loss, and is therein an example to princes and great men, teaching them to lay much to heart the calamities that befall the public; he is also a type of Christ, to whom the blood of his subjects is precious. He rent his clothes in token of great sorrow for this public disaster, and especially in dread of God's displeasure, which was certainly the cause of it; had it been but the common chance of war, as we are too apt to express it, it would not have become a general to droop thus under it, but when God was angry it was his duty and honour to feel thus, one of the bravest soldiers that ever was having owned that his flesh trembled for fear of God. As one humbling himself under the mighty hand of God he fell to the earth upon his face, not thinking it any disparagement to him to lie thus low before the great God, to whom he directed this token of reverence by keeping his eye towards the ark of the Lord; and the elders of Israel, being interested in the cause, joined him.

Clarke says it was not in consequence of this slight discomfiture, simply considered in itself, that Joshua laid the business so much to heart, but because the people melted and became as water, and there was little hope that they would make any stand against the enemy. Of the cry he observes that particles of exclamation and distress, or what are called interjections, are nearly the same in all languages, the reason being that they are the simple voice of nature, and he gives the Hebrew word which is translated alas. The complaint of Joshua in this and the following verses seems to him to have arisen principally from his deep concern for the glory of God and the affecting interest he took in the people: he felt for the thousands of Israel, whom he considered as abandoned to destruction, and he felt for the glory of God, since he knew that should Israel be destroyed God's name would be blasphemed among the heathen; and his expostulations with his Maker, which have been too hastily blamed by some as savouring of too great freedom and impatience, are founded on God's own words in Deuteronomy and on the practice of Moses himself, who had used similar expressions. Wesley says the clothes were rent in testimony of great sorrow, for the loss felt, the consequent mischief feared, and the sin which he suspected, and that Joshua lay on his face in deep humiliation and fervent supplication, continuing the whole day in fasting and prayer. Of the complaint he says that this and the following clause, though well intended, yet savour of human infirmity and fall short of that reverence and modesty and submission which Joshua owed to God, and are mentioned as instances that the holy men of God were subject to like passions and infirmities with ourselves. The question what he shall say he takes as asked in answer to the reproaches of insulting enemies, and Israel as God's people, whom he had singled out of all nations for his own; and the great name he says would on this occasion be blasphemed and charged with inconstancy and with inability to resist them or to do his people that good which he intended, so that whatever happens we ought to pray that God's name be not blasphemed, since it is a great name, above every name.

Ellicott says the words of Joshua and his behaviour on this occasion are consistent with all that we read of him, and confirm the notion that he was not a man of a naturally daring and adventurous spirit but inclined to distrust his own powers, and yet utterly indomitable and unflinching in the discharge of his duty, a man of moral rather than physical courage. Of the fear that the Canaanites would environ them round he says it was a thing extremely probable in itself, apart from the supernatural character of the invasion. Keil's blocks on this span are chiefly verse quotation, recording Joshua's expostulation and the Lord's answer bidding him rise.

debates: Whether Joshua's expostulation was blameworthy: Wesley says the words savour of human infirmity and fall short of the reverence and submission he owed, Clarke says they have been too hastily blamed and are founded on God's own words in Deuteronomy and on the practice of Moses, and Calvin divides the prayer, calling it partly the fruit of faith and partly of excessive perturbation

Why so small a loss prostrated the general: Calvin raises the objection that it ill became a courageous leader and answers that Joshua could not fall back on the doubtful fortune of war, since God had promised constant victory, while Clarke points to the melting of the people and Henry to the anger of God rather than the chance of war

What the mourning rites meant: Gill takes them as the ancient custom on hearing bad news, Calvin allows that the heathen used them too but makes them here a profession of repentance in deprecating God's wrath, and Henry reads the posture as humbling under the mighty hand of God with the eye toward the ark

What kind of man Joshua was: Ellicott infers from this behaviour that he was not naturally daring but inclined to distrust his own powers, yet indomitable in duty, a man of moral rather than physical courage

What the plea about the great name urges: Gill makes it a vindication of God's power and faithfulness against the enemy's charge, Wesley that the name would be charged with inconstancy and inability, and Calvin adds the separate fear that the quiet nations would take courage and attack
outliers: Clarke's defence of Joshua against critics he calls too hasty, grounded on Deuteronomy and on the practice of Moses
Calvin's division of a single prayer into a part springing from faith and a part from excessive perturbation
Ellicott's character sketch of Joshua as a man of moral rather than physical courage
Clarke's observation that interjections are nearly the same in all languages, being the simple voice of nature
Henry's likening of Joshua to Christ, to whom the blood of his subjects is precious
Calvin's remark that Joshua could not console himself with the doubtfulness of war because he had a promise of unbroken victory
Wesley's rule that whatever happens we ought to pray that God's name be not blasphemed

10.pericope_label: God’s answer: Israel has sinned, and the people must be sanctified

schools.summary: Gill says God bade Joshua get up from the ground where he lay prostrate, not as refusing his supplication but rather as encouraging and strengthening him, and chiefly in order to instruct him. Of the charge against Israel he says that though one only had committed the sin, others might have known of it and connived at it; however, there was sin committed among them, and it must be discovered, the guilt charged and punishment inflicted. The children of Israel could not stand before their enemies, he says, being forsaken of God for the sin committed among them. In the command to sanctify the people he notes that the word up signifies not only getting up from the ground on which Joshua lay but bestirring himself and being active in what he was now to be enjoined. Calvin says God does not reprimand Joshua absolutely for lying prostrate on the ground and lamenting the overthrow of the people, since the true method of obtaining pardon from God was to fall down suppliantly before him, but for giving himself up to excessive sorrow; and the censure ought to be referred to the future rather than to the past, for he tells him to put an end to his wailing, just as if he had said that he had already lain too long prostrate and that all sloth must now be abandoned, since there was need of a different remedy. He first shows the cause of the evil and then prescribes the mode of removing it, informing him that the issue of the battle was disastrous because he was offended with the wickedness of the people and had cast off their defence. Why the punishment of a private sacrilege is transferred to all he has explained before; although they were not held guilty in their own judgment or that of others, the judgment of God, which involved them in the same condemnation, had hidden reasons into which, though it may perhaps be lawful to inquire soberly, it is not lawful to search with prying curiosity. At the same time we have a rare example of clemency in the fact that, while the condemnation verbally extends to all, punishment is inflicted only on a single family actually polluted by the crime. On the command to sanctify he says that although the word has a more extensive meaning, yet as the subject in question is the expiation of the people he has no doubt that it prescribes a formal rite of sanctification, so that those who interpret it generally do not give it its full force; as they were now to be in a manner brought into the divine presence, there was need of purification that they might not come while unclean. Though the ceremony might be in itself of little consequence, it had a powerful tendency to arouse a rude people: the external offering must have turned their thoughts to spiritual cleanness, while their abstinence from things otherwise lawful reminded them of the very high and unblemished purity which was required. They are forewarned of what is to take place in order that each may be more careful in examining himself; nay, the Lord proceeds step by step, as if he meant to give intervals for repentance, for it is impossible to imagine any other reason for descending from tribe to family and coming at length to the single man.

Henry says God's answer came from the oracle over the ark, before which Joshua had prostrated himself, and that those who desire to know the will of God must attend with their desires upon the lively oracles and wait at wisdom's gates for wisdom's dictates; let those who find themselves under the tokens of God's displeasure never complain of him but complain to him, and they shall receive an answer of peace, the answer here coming immediately while Joshua was yet speaking. God encourages Joshua against his present despondencies and the black and melancholy apprehensions he had of the posture of Israel's affairs, bidding him not suffer his spirits to droop and sink. No doubt Joshua did well to humble himself before God and mourn under the tokens of his displeasure, but now God told him it was enough and would not have him continue any longer in that melancholy posture, for God delights not in the grief of penitents when they afflict their souls further than as it qualifies them for pardon.

Clarke says it is plain there was nothing in Joshua's prayer or complaint that was offensive to God, for here there is no reprehension: the question why he lies thus means only that this is no time for complaint, since something else is indispensably necessary to be done. It is impossible, he says, that God should turn against his people if they had not turned away from him: they have taken of the accursed thing notwithstanding the severe prohibition, and they have also stolen, supposing that if they were not seen by their brethren God would either not see or not notice. From the statement that they were accursed he infers that the nature of the execration or anathema was such that those who took of the thing doomed to destruction fell immediately under the same condemnation, the inhabitants of Jericho and all that they had being accursed. The command to sanctify the people he explains as a charge to cause them to wash themselves and get into a proper disposition to hear the judgment of the Lord relative to the late transaction, Joshua having lain prostrate before the ark all the time that God spoke. Wesley says the business is not to be done by inactive supplication but by vigorous endeavours for reformation. Israel he takes as some or one of them, and the transgression of the covenant as the breaking of conditions they had promised to perform, whereof this was one, not to meddle with the accursed thing; the stealing was the taking of God's portion which he had reserved. That they were accursed means they had put themselves out of God's protection and were therefore liable to the same destruction which belonged to the accursed people. To sanctify themselves is to purify themselves from that defilement which they had all in some sort contracted by this accursed fact, and to prepare themselves to appear before the Lord, expecting the sentence of God for the discovery and punishment of the sin.

Ellicott renders the question as, why is this, that thou art fallen upon thy face, and notes that the pronoun is emphatic. On the transgression of the covenant he says the law is again brought prominently forward in this scene, since the words of the covenant, the ten commandments, are first of all a pledge that Jehovah is the God of Israel who brought them out of the land of Egypt; and he brought them out that he might bring them in, and made them the executioners of his wrath against the idolaters. They must have no other gods but him, and they must not treat the things that had been defiled by association with idolatry as their own spoil; the words which specially apply to this case are found in Deuteronomy, that the graven images of their gods shall be burnt with fire and that they shall not desire the silver or gold upon them, nor bring an abomination into the house lest they become a cursed thing like it. The whole spoil of Canaan was not so treated, he adds, but concerning that of Jericho there had been express orders, possibly because the city was especially defiled with idolatry; God had proclaimed it abomination, it was a devoted or accursed thing, and no Israelite was to appropriate any of it under penalty of becoming accursed himself. Keil says Israel had sinned, and that very grievously, in transgressing the covenant by taking of the accursed thing, stealing, dissembling and putting it among their own stuff; on account of this sin the Israelites could not stand before their enemies but turned their backs, because they were themselves accursed, and God would not be with them any more except they destroyed the accursed from among them.

debates: Whether God rebuked Joshua at all: Clarke denies any reprehension, Gill hears encouragement and instruction, Henry allows the mourning but says God called it enough, and Calvin distinguishes the prostration, which was right, from the excessive sorrow, and refers the censure to the future rather than the past

Why the whole nation is charged for one man's theft: Calvin, having attempted an explanation at the chapter's opening, here withdraws to hidden reasons into which it is not lawful to search with prying curiosity, while noting the clemency by which the punishment fell on one family only; Gill keeps the possibility that others knew and connived

Why the spoil of Jericho in particular was forbidden: Ellicott grounds it in the covenant and in the Deuteronomic prohibition against desiring the silver or gold on the images, and suggests the city was especially defiled with idolatry, while Clarke infers from the word itself that whoever took the devoted thing became devoted

What sanctifying the people required: Calvin insists on a formal rite of purification and says those who take the word generally do not give it its full force, while Clarke reduces it to washing and a proper disposition and Wesley to purifying from a defilement all had in some sort contracted

Why the lot descended by stages: Calvin says the Lord proceeded step by step as if to give intervals for repentance, since no other reason can be imagined for descending from tribe to family before reaching the man
outliers: Calvin's retreat from explanation to hidden reasons, into which it may be lawful to inquire soberly but not to search with prying curiosity
Calvin's rare example of clemency, that the verbal condemnation extends to all while the punishment falls on one family
Calvin's account of the ceremony as of little consequence in itself yet powerfully rousing to a rude people
Clarke's reconstruction of the thief's calculation, that if his brethren did not see, God would either not see or not notice
Ellicott's emphasis on the pronoun, why is this that thou art fallen upon thy face
Henry's rule that those under the tokens of God's displeasure should never complain of him but complain to him
Henry's observation that God delights not in the grief of penitents beyond what qualifies them for pardon

schools.summary: Gill says that in the morning one or more of every tribe, according to the number of them, were to be brought before Joshua and the elders of Israel, the sanhedrim and council of the nation, and very probably the tabernacle, where they assembled for this purpose. Of the sentence he says that he who is taken by lot, and the accursed thing found with him, should die by burning, one of the four capital punishments with the Jews; this was ordered in this case because the city of Jericho, accursed or devoted, was burnt with fire. That Joshua rose up early in the morning showed his readiness and diligence to obey the command of God; and as there was much work to do, it required that he should rise early. He takes the family of Judah, with Kimchi and Ben Melech, to mean the tribe of Judah, or rather the several families in that tribe, even the heads of them; and the household brought man by man he takes to be the household of Zabdi, the heads of each house therein.

Henry says the discovery of Achan by the lot proved a perfect lot, though it proceeded gradually; and though Joshua may have slept the better for knowing the worst of the disease of that body of which under God he was the head, he rose up early, so much was his heart upon it to put away the accursed thing, which shows his zeal and vehement desire to see Israel restored to the divine favour. In the scrutiny he observes first that the guilty tribe was that of Judah, which was, and was to be, of all the tribes the most honourable and illustrious; this was an alloy to their dignity and might serve as a check to their pride, for many there were who were its glories, but here was one that was its reproach. Let not the best families think it strange if there be those found in them, and descending from them, that prove their grief and shame. Judah was to have the first and largest lot in Canaan, and the more inexcusable is one of that tribe if, not content to wait for his own share, he break in upon God's property. The Jews' tradition, he adds, is that when the tribe of Judah was taken the valiant men of that tribe drew their swords and professed they would not sheathe them again till they saw the criminal punished and themselves cleared, who knew their own innocency. Secondly, the guilty person was at length fastened upon, and the language of the lot was, Thou art the man. It was strange that Achan, being conscious to himself of guilt, when he saw the lot come nearer and nearer to him, had not either the wit to make an escape or the grace to make a confession; but his heart was hardened through the deceitfulness of sin, and it proved to be to his own destruction. We may well imagine how his countenance changed, and what horror and confusion seized him when he was singled out as the delinquent, when the eyes of all Israel were fastened upon him, and every one was ready to say, Have we found thee, O our enemy? See here the folly of those that promise themselves secrecy in sin: the righteous God has many ways of bringing to light the hidden works of darkness, and so bringing to shame and ruin those that continue their fellowship with those unfruitful works; a bird of the air, when God pleases, shall carry the voice. See also how much it is our concern, when God is contending with us, to find out what the particular sin is that, like Achan, troubles our camp; we must examine ourselves and carefully review the records of conscience, and pray earnestly with holy Job, Lord, show me wherefore thou contendest with me.

Clarke says it has been a subject of serious inquiry in what manner and by what means the culpable tribe, family, household and individual were discovered. The Jews have many conceits on the subject, the most rational being that the tribes, in their representatives, being brought before the high priest, the stone on the breastplate gave immediate intimation by suddenly losing its lustre; according to them this is what is termed consulting God by Urim and Thummim. It is however most probable, he says, that the whole was determined by the lot, and that God chose this method to detect the guilty tribe, next the family, thirdly the household, and lastly the individual; this was nearly the plan pursued in the election of Saul by Samuel, where the tribe of Benjamin was taken, then the family of Matri, then Saul the son of Kish, and if the lot was used in the one case it was doubtless used in the other also, the procedure in the main being entirely similar. The same mode was used to find out who had transgressed the king's command when Jonathan had eaten a little honey; the promised land was divided by lot; the courses of the priests were regulated by lot in the days of David; and that this was a frequent mode of determining difficult questions, and appointed by God himself, is evident from Leviticus, the Psalms, Proverbs and Acts. On the following verse he reports Kennicott at length: all Israel came near by tribes and one tribe was fixed on, then that tribe came by its families and one family was fixed on, then came that family by its households and one household was fixed on, and then that household coming man by man, one man was fixed on; yet according to the present text, in the execution of this command all Israel came and the tribe of Judah was fixed on, secondly came the families of Judah and the family of the Zarhites was fixed on, thirdly came the family of the Zarhites man by man and Zabdi was fixed on, and fourthly came the household of Zabdi man by man and Achan was fixed on, so that in the third article the word for by households is most certainly left out and the fourth article, man by man, is improperly expressed twice; the true word by households is preserved in six Hebrew copies and the Syriac version. By this method was discovered Achan, as he is here five times called, though the valley in which he was stoned is called Achor; he is also called Achar in the text and in all the versions in the Chronicles, and Achar in the five places of Joshua in the Syriac version, in all five in the Greek of the Vatican manuscript and twice in the Alexandrian. Wesley says the Lord taketh means the one who shall be declared guilty by the lot, which is disposed by the Lord, and which was to be cast in the Lord's presence before the ark; of such use of lots he cites the case of Jonathan, of Jonah and of the apostles. He that is taken shall be burnt with fire, as persons and things accursed were to be, and all that he hath means his children and goods, according to the law in Deuteronomy. Wrought folly: so sin is often called in scripture, in opposition to the idle opinion of sinners, who commonly esteem it to be their wisdom; and in Israel means among the church and people of God who had such excellent laws to direct them, and such an all-sufficient and gracious God to provide for them, without any such unworthy practices. It was sacrilege, it was invading God's rights and converting to a private use that which was devoted to his glory, which was to be thus severely punished, for a warning to all people in all ages to take heed how they rob God. On the seventeenth verse he takes the family to mean either the tribe or people, as the word family sometimes signifies, or the families, the singular number for the plural, the chief of each of their five families; and man by man he takes to mean not every individual person, as is evident from the next verse, but every head of the several houses or lesser families of that greater family of the Zarhites.

Ellicott says there is nothing in the language of the passage, when closely considered, which would lead us to suppose that the discovery of the criminal was by casting lots. The parallel passage, the selection of King Saul from the tribes of Israel, shows that the oracle of God was consulted: they inquired, and the Lord answered; so it was, perhaps, in the case of Achan. We seem to see the high priest of Israel asking counsel for Joshua after the judgment of Urim before the Lord, as it had been foretold in Numbers, and the elders of Israel standing by at the door of the tabernacle of the congregation; the representatives of the tribes enter the sacred enclosure in succession and pass before the high priest in awful silence, broken only by the voice of Jehovah, who pronounces at intervals the names of Judah, Zarhite, Zabdi, Carmi, Achan. It must have been a terrible ordeal, but all present must have felt that no human partiality or private animosity was seeking its victim, and that the Judge of all the earth was doing judgment. When the accusation of Jehovah was followed by the explicit confession of the criminal, and this again by the discovery of the stolen spoil of Jericho, which was brought in and poured out before the Lord, and when this was followed by the execution of the awful sentence, all who were present must have received a lesson which it was impossible to forget as to the reality of the covenant of God. And if, as seems most probable, the voice of the oracle was uttered from the inner sanctuary, from between the cherubim, but heard even to the outer court as the voice of the Almighty God when he speaketh, we learn once more the majesty of the law given to Israel; the arrest of Jordan, the overthrow of Jericho and the discovery of Achan are all manifestations of power proceeding from the same source. Keil says that at the seventeenth verse we should expect the tribe or the families of Judah instead of the family; the plural is adopted in the Septuagint and Vulgate and is also to be met with in seven manuscripts, but this is a conjecture rather than the original reading, since the word is either used generally or employed in a collective sense. On Joshua's address to Achan he says that when Achan had been discovered to be the criminal, Joshua charged him to give honour and praise to the Lord and to confess without reserve what he had done; it is not ironically or with dissimulation that Joshua addresses him as my son, but with sincere paternal regard, and he quotes Calvin's remark that this example serves as a lesson to judges, that when punishing crimes they should moderate their rigour and not lose all the feelings of humanity, and on the other hand that whilst merciful they should not be careless or remiss.

debates: Whether the discovery was by lot or by the oracle: Clarke judges it most probable that the whole was determined by the lot and cites the election of Saul, while Ellicott says there is nothing in the language to suggest lots and takes the very same passage to show that the oracle of God was consulted; Wesley sides with the lot, disposed by the Lord and cast before the ark

Whether the text of the search is sound: Clarke, following Kennicott, holds that by households has dropped out of the third article and man by man is doubled, six Hebrew copies and the Syriac preserving the true word; Keil calls the plural of the Septuagint, Vulgate and seven manuscripts a conjecture rather than the original reading; Wesley harmonises without emendation by taking the singular for the plural

What man by man means: Clarke and Kennicott take it as a corruption in one of the two places where it stands, while Wesley takes it as heads of houses rather than individuals, which he argues the next verse proves
outliers: Clarke's report of the Jewish conceit that the stone on the breastplate gave intimation by suddenly losing its lustre
Ellicott's reconstruction of the scene, the tribes passing in awful silence broken only by the voice pronouncing Judah, Zarhite, Zabdi, Carmi, Achan
Ellicott's suggestion that the voice was uttered from between the cherubim yet heard to the outer court, so that Jordan, Jericho and Achan are one power
Henry's note that Judah, the most honourable tribe and heir to the first and largest lot, would not wait for its own share
The Jewish tradition Henry passes on, that Judah's valiant men drew their swords and would not sheathe them till the criminal was punished and they were cleared
Keil's quotation of Calvin on judges, that they should moderate their rigour without becoming careless or remiss
Kennicott's tally of Achar against Achan across the Syriac, Vatican and Alexandrian copies

19.pericope_label: Achan confesses, and the spoil is found

schools.summary: Gill says Joshua treated Achan in a very humane, affectionate and respectable manner, though so great a criminal, being a subject of his and of the same religion and nation; that Achan made a free and open confession of his sin; and that the messengers were sent directly to Achan's tent to see if it was as he had said and to bring the things with them, taking them out of the place, hole or pit in which they were hid. Of the garment he says it was one only, as the Targum adds, for no more was taken: a garment made of Babylonish wool, as Jarchi, or a valuable garment made in Babylon, called Shinar, for that is the word in the text, so Kimchi and Abarbanel; and Babylonian garments were in great esteem in other nations. Pliny says Babylon was famous for garments interwoven with pictures of divers colours, which gave name to them; and Plutarch relates that Cato in his great modesty, being an enemy to luxury, having a Babylonish garment that came to him by inheritance, ordered it immediately to be sold. The Vulgate Latin version calls it a scarlet robe, and in some Jewish writings it is interpreted a garment of Babylonian purple, as if it only respected the colour; purple and scarlet are sometimes used promiscuously, and were the colour worn by kings. Josephus calls it a royal garment, wholly interwoven with gold, and some have thought it the garment of the king of Jericho, which is not unlikely. Calvin says that although Achan is caught only by lot, which seems to fall out fortuitously, yet since God had declared that he would point out the guilty party as if with the finger, Joshua interrogates without any doubt and urges him to confess. It is probable that this was the usual form of adjuration, as the scribes and priests used the same words in adjuring the blind man whose sight our Saviour had restored; but there was a special reason why Joshua exhorted Achan to give God the glory, because by denying or equivocating he might have impaired the credit of the decision, the matter having already been determined by lot. Joshua therefore simply orders him to subscribe to the divine sentence and not aggravate the crime by vain denials. He calls him son neither ironically nor hypocritically, but truly and sincerely declares that he felt like a father toward him whom he had already doomed to death. By this example judges are taught that, while they punish crimes, they ought so to temper their severity as not to lay aside the feelings of humanity, and on the other hand that they ought to be merciful without being reckless and remiss; that in short they ought to be as parents to those they condemn, without substituting undue mildness for the sternness of justice. Many by fawning kindness throw wretched criminals off their guard, pretending that they mean to pardon them, and then, after a confession has been extracted, suddenly hand them over to the executioner, while they were flattering themselves with the hope of impunity; but Joshua, satisfied with having cited the criminal before the tribunal of God, does not at all flatter him with a vain hope of pardon, and is thus more at liberty to pronounce the sentence which God has dictated. Of the confession he says that Achan, now struck with astonishment, neither employs subterfuge nor palliates the crime nor endeavours to give any colouring to it, but rather ingenuously details the whole matter; thus the sacred name of God was more effectual in extorting a confession than any tortures could have been. Nor was the simplicity he thus displayed a sure indication of repentance; being as it were overcome with terror, he openly divulged what he would willingly have concealed. It is no new thing for the wicked, after they have endeavoured for some time to escape and have even grown hardened in vice, to become voluntary witnesses against themselves, not properly of their own accord but because God drags them against their will and in a manner drives them headlong; and this open answer will condemn the hypocrisy of many who obscure the clear light by their subterfuges. The expression is emphatic, thus and thus did I, meaning that each part of the transaction was explained distinctly and in order; nor does he only acknowledge the deed, but by renouncing all defence and throwing aside all pretext he condemns himself in regard to its atrocity. I have sinned, he says; this he would not have said had he not been conscious of sacrilege, and hence it appears that he did not pretend mistake or want of thought. Of the messengers Calvin says that although it is not singular for messengers to prove their obedience by running and making haste, the haste here mentioned shows how intent all were to have the work of expiation performed as speedily as possible, since they had been filled with the greatest anxiety by the stern denunciation that God would not be with them until they were purged of the anathema; they therefore ran swiftly, not merely to execute the commands of Joshua but much more to appease the Lord. The things carried off by stealth, when placed before their eyes, were more than sufficient to explain the cause of the disgrace and overthrow which had befallen them; and they were reminded how much importance God attached to the delivery of the first-fruits of the whole land of Canaan in an untainted state, in order that his liberality might never perish from their memory. They also learned that while the knowledge of God penetrates to the most hidden recesses, it is in vain to employ concealments for the purpose of eluding his judgment.

Clarke says that, the person being now detected, Joshua wishes him to acknowledge the omniscience of God and confess his crime; this was designed not only for the edification of the people and a vindication of the righteous judgment of God, but in reference to his own salvation, for as his life was now become forfeited to the law there was the utmost necessity of humiliation before God that his soul might be saved. Give glory to God signifies the same as, make a thorough confession as in the presence of God, and disguise no part of the truth; in this way and in these very words the Jews adjured the man who had been born blind that he would truly tell who had healed him, for they pretended to believe that Christ was such a sinner that God would not work a miracle by him. Of the confession he says this seems a very honest and hearty confession, and there is hope that this poor culprit escaped perdition. Of the garment he says the word means a splendid or costly robe of Shinar, but as Babylon was built in the plain of Shinar the word has in general been translated Babylon in this place; it is very probable that this was the robe of the king of Jericho, for the same word is used of the royal robe of the king of Nineveh which he laid aside in order to humble himself before God. Bochart and Calmet have shown at large that Babylonish robes were very splendid and in high reputation; they are generally allowed to have been of various colours, though some suppose they were woven thus, others that they were embroidered with the needle, and others that they were painted. Silius Italicus appears to think they were woven thus, Martial seems to say they were embroidered with the needle, and Pliny and Apuleius speak of them as if painted; but it may be observed that the clothes woven of divers colours at Babylon appear rather to have had the pictures woven or embroidered in them than painted on them, though it is most likely the figures referred to were the work of the needle after the cloth came from the loom. Aquila translates the original by a Babylonish robe, Symmachus by a robe of Synar, the Septuagint by a fine garment of different colours, and the Vulgate by a scarlet cloak; there is no doubt it was both beautiful and costly, and on these grounds it was coveted by Achan. Two hundred shekels of silver, at three shillings per shekel, amount to about thirty pounds sterling; a wedge of gold is a tongue of gold, what we commonly call an ingot, a corruption of the word lingot signifying a little tongue, of fifty shekels weight, which would be worth about a hundred and thirteen pounds. This verse, he says, gives us a notable instance of the progress of sin: it enters by the eye, sinks into the heart, actuates the hand, and leads to secrecy and dissimulation; I saw, I coveted, I took and hid them in the earth. Thus says St James, when lust is conceived it bringeth forth sin, and when sin is finished it bringeth forth death. Wesley says Joshua calls him son to show that this severe inquisition and sentence did not proceed from any hatred to his person, whom he loved as a father doth his son, and as a prince ought to do each of his subjects. As thou hast highly dishonoured the Lord God of Israel, now take the blame to thyself and ascribe unto God the glory of his omniscience in knowing thy sin, of his justice in punishing it in thee and others for thy sake, of his omnipotency which was obstructed by thee, and of his kindness and faithfulness to his people which was eclipsed by thy wickedness, all which will now be evident by thy sin confessed and punished. He seems, says Wesley, to make a sincere and ingenuous confession, and loads his sin with all just aggravations: against the Lord, that is, against his express command and glorious attributes; the God of Israel, the true God, who hath chosen me and all Israel to be the people of his peculiar love and care. Of the garment he says such were composed with great art with divers colours and of great price, as appears both from scripture and heathen authors; the two hundred shekels were in weight, not in coin, for as yet they received and paid money by weight; and the silver under it means under the Babylonish garment, covered with it or wrapt up in it. He accurately describes the progress of his sin, which began at his eye, which he permitted to gaze upon them, which inflamed his desire and made him covet them, and that desire made him take them, and having taken, resolve to keep them, and to that end hide them in his tent. The messengers were sent that the truth of his confession might be unquestionable, which some peradventure might think was forced from him; and they ran partly longing to free themselves and all the people from the curse under which they lay, and partly that none of Achan's relations might get thither before them and take away the things. Before the Lord means where Joshua and the elders continued yet in their assembly, waiting for the issue.

Ellicott says we can hardly read these words of Joshua without being reminded of his great Antitype: in New Testament language, to tell Joshua is to tell Jesus, the only way in which confession of sin can bring glory. Joshua could only pronounce sentence of death on Achan, but if we confess our sins he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness; and the Hebrew word for confession also means thanksgiving, so that acknowledgment of sin and mercy are not far apart in making confession to God. Of the garment he says it is literally a certain goodly mantle of Shinar; and of the coveting, that the very word employed is that used not only in the tenth commandment but also in the passage of Deuteronomy which forbids Israel to desire the spoils of idolatry, a coincidence of terms which makes it somewhat probable that the whole were found in some idol's temple and were part of the spoils of the shrine. On the laying out of the spoil he says the silver and the gold, by God's order, should have been brought into his treasury; the spoils of Canaan might have been consecrated as holiness to Jehovah, but in this instance the spoil of Jericho had become the sin of Israel, and it must therefore be no longer preserved but consumed. Keil says Achan acknowledged his sin and confessed that he had appropriated to himself from among the booty a beautiful Babylonish cloak, two hundred shekels of silver and a tongue of gold of fifty shekels weight; a Babylonish cloak, literally a cloak of Shinar or Babylon, is a costly cloak, artistically worked, such as were manufactured in Babylon and distributed far and wide through the medium of commerce, Pliny recording that Babylon above all made famous the weaving of various colours into cloth and gave the practice its name. The Septuagint rendering means a Babylonian cloak ornamented with pictures, called smooth because it was cut smooth and figured because it was covered with coloured figures, either of men or animals, sometimes woven and at other times worked with the needle. Joshua sent two messengers directly to Achan's tent to fetch the things, and when they were brought he had them laid down before Jehovah, that is, before the tabernacle, where the whole affair had taken place; the verb used here and in Samuel signifies to lay down, whilst another form is used for pouring out.

debates: Whether Achan's confession was repentance: Clarke calls it honest and hearty and hopes he escaped perdition, and Wesley calls it sincere and ingenuous, while Calvin denies that the simplicity was any sure indication of repentance, since terror made him divulge what he would willingly have concealed and God drags such witnesses against their will

How the Babylonish robe was made: Clarke reports Silius Italicus for weaving, Martial for the needle and Pliny and Apuleius as though painted, and decides for needlework after the loom, while Keil takes the Septuagint rendering to cover both woven and needled figures

What the robe was: Gill and Clarke both incline to the king of Jericho's garment, Josephus calling it royal and interwoven with gold, while Ellicott's argument from the word coveted points instead to the spoils of an idol's shrine

What giving glory to God meant: Clarke and Calvin take it as the standard form of adjuration used later against the man born blind, Wesley unfolds it into four dishonoured attributes, and Ellicott reads it forward to confession made to Christ
outliers: Calvin's warning against judges who use fawning kindness to extract a confession and then hand the prisoner to the executioner
Calvin's rule that judges should be as parents to those they condemn without substituting undue mildness for the sternness of justice
Calvin's account of the messengers running not merely to obey Joshua but to appease the Lord
Clarke's four-step anatomy of sin, entering by the eye, sinking into the heart, actuating the hand and leading to dissimulation
Ellicott's note that the Hebrew for confession also means thanksgiving
Ellicott's inference from the word coveted that the spoil came from an idol's shrine
Plutarch's Cato, reported by Gill, selling an inherited Babylonish garment out of enmity to luxury

schools.summary: Gill says Joshua and all Israel are mentioned to show the perfect agreement between Joshua and the heads of the people in this affair of Achan, and in the nature and manner of his punishment; and that Joshua's question means, thou hast been the occasion of so much trouble to us by committing this sin. Of the heap he says that at the place where he suffered, or where they laid his ashes, they heaped up a pile of stones over him as a monument whereby it might be known hereafter where he was executed and buried, and which pile continued to the writing of this history; such funeral monuments were usual with the heathens also as well as with the Jews. That the Lord turned from the fierceness of his anger means that the effects of it ceased, the outward face of things was altered and the dealings of God in his providence with Israel were changed; though, properly speaking, there is no change in God, nor such affections and passions in him as in man. Calvin says Achan is led without the camp for two reasons: first, that it might not be tainted and polluted by the execution, as God always required that some trace of humanity should remain even in the infliction of legitimate punishments, and secondly, that no defilement might remain among the people. It was customary to inflict punishment without the camp, that the people might have a greater abhorrence at the shedding of blood; but now a rotten member is cut off from the body, and the camp is purified from pollution, and the example became memorable, as it gave its name to the spot. If any one is disturbed and offended by the severity of the punishment, he must always be brought back to this point, that though our reason dissent from the judgments of God, we must check our presumption by the curb of a pious modesty and soberness, and not disapprove whatever does not please us. It seems harsh, nay barbarous and inhuman, that young children, without fault, should be hurried off to cruel execution, to be stoned and burned; that dumb animals should be treated in the same manner is not so strange, as they were created for the sake of men and thus deservedly follow the fate of their owners, and everything which Achan possessed perished with him as an accessory. But it seems a cruel vengeance to stone and burn children for the crime of their father, and here God publicly inflicts punishment on children for the sake of their parents, contrary to what he declares by Ezekiel. How it is that he destroys no one who is innocent, and visits the sins of fathers upon children, Calvin says he explained when speaking of the common destruction of Jericho and the promiscuous slaughter of all ages: the infants who then perished by the sword we bewail as unworthily slain, as they had no apparent fault, but if we consider how much more deeply divine knowledge penetrates than human intellect can possibly do, we will rather acquiesce in his decree than hurry ourselves to a precipice by giving way to presumption and extravagant pride. It was certainly not owing to reckless hatred that the sons of Achan were pitilessly slain: not only were they the creatures of God's hand, but circumcision, the infallible symbol of adoption, was engraved on their flesh, and yet he adjudges them to death. What here remains for us but to acknowledge our weakness and submit to his incomprehensible counsel? It may be that death proved to them a medicine; but if they were reprobate, then condemnation could not be premature. From the enumeration of Achan's oxen, asses and sheep, he adds, we gather that he was sufficiently rich, and that therefore it was not poverty that urged him to the crime; it must be regarded as a proof of his insatiable cupidity that he coveted stolen articles, not for use but for luxury. Of Joshua's words at the execution Calvin says the invective seems excessively harsh, as if it had been his intention to drive the wretched man to frantic madness when he ought rather to have exhorted him to patience; he has no doubt that Joshua spoke thus for the sake of the people, in order to furnish a useful example to all, not wishing to overwhelm Achan with despair but only to show in his person how grievous a crime it is to disturb the Church of God. It may be, however, that the haughty Achan complained that his satisfaction, by which he thought he had sufficiently discharged himself, was not accepted, and that Joshua inveighed thus bitterly with the view of correcting or breaking his contumacy; the question seems to imply that he was expostulating, and when he appeals to God as judge he seems to be silencing an obstinate man. The throwing of stones by the whole people was a general sign of detestation, by which they declared that they had no share in the crime which they thus avenged, and that they held it in abhorrence. The heap of stones was intended partly as a memorial to posterity, and partly to prevent any one from imprudently gathering particles of gold or silver on the spot, if it had remained unoccupied; for although the Lord had previously ordered that the gold of Jericho should be offered to him, he would not allow his sanctuary to be polluted by the proceeds of theft.

Clarke says Achan and his cattle and substance were brought to the valley to be consumed, his sons and daughters probably to witness the judgments of God inflicted on their disobedient parent. On Joshua's question he notes the reference to the meaning of Achan's or Achar's name, and that since the verb used here and the valley's name both have the second form, some have supposed Achar was his proper name, as it is read in the Chronicles and in some manuscripts and ancient versions. With great deference to the judgment of others, he asks, can it be fairly proved from the text that the sons and daughters of Achan were stoned to death and burnt as well as their father? The text certainly leaves it doubtful, but seems rather to intimate that Achan alone was stoned and that his substance was burnt with fire: the present Hebrew reads, they stoned him with stones and burnt them with fire after they had stoned them with stones, the singular in the first clause and the plural in the last leaving the matter doubtful. The Vulgate is very clear, that all Israel stoned him and all that he had was consumed with fire; the Septuagint adds this and the first clause of the next verse together, that all Israel stoned him with stones and raised over him a great heap of stones; the Syriac says simply that they stoned him with stones and burned what pertained to him with fire; the Targum is the same as the Hebrew; the Anglo-Saxon seems to refer the whole to Achan and his goods; the Arabic version alone says they stoned him and his children and his goods. Instead of burnt them, two of De Rossi's manuscripts read him, which reading, if genuine, would make the different members of the verse agree better. It is possible, he says, that Achan, his oxen, asses, sheep, tent and all his household goods were destroyed, but his sons and daughters left uninjured; and if it be asked why they were brought out into the valley with the rest, it was that they might see and fear, and be for ever deterred by their father's punishment from imitating his example. He has gone thus far into this important transaction, in which the justice and mercy of God are so much concerned, that he might assign to each its due. That Achan's life was forfeited to justice by his transgression no one doubts, for he sinned against a known and positive law; his children could not suffer with him because of the law in Deuteronomy, unless they had been accomplices in his guilt, of which there is no evidence, and the text which speaks of Achan's punishment is extremely dubious as far as it relates to this point. One circumstance that strengthens the supposition that the children were not included is the command that he who is taken with the accursed thing shall be burnt with fire, he and all that he hath: all that he hath may certainly refer to his goods and not to his children, and his punishment and the destruction of his property would answer every purpose of public justice, both as a punishment and preventive of the crime; and both mercy and justice require that the innocent shall not suffer with the guilty, unless in very extraordinary cases. In the case before us no necessity of this kind urged it, and therefore he concludes that Achan alone suffered, that his repentance and confession were genuine and sincere, and that while justice required his life, mercy was extended to the salvation of his soul. Of the heap he says the burial places both of heroes and of eminent culprits were anciently thus distinguished, and transactions of this kind gave rise to those great piles of stones called cairns, so frequently met with in northern countries. From the whole account we may see the exceeding sinfulness of sin and the great danger of not withstanding its first approaches: by covetousness many lives and many souls have been destroyed, and yet the living lay it not to heart. Who fears the love of money, provided he can get riches? Through the intensity of this desire every part of the surface of the earth, and as far as possible its bowels, are ransacked in order to get wealth, and God alone can tell to how many private crimes, frauds and dissimulations this gives birth, by which the wrath of God is brought down upon the community at large. The sinner against his God is an enemy to his country: an open foe may be resisted and repelled because he is known, but the covetous man is an unseen pestilence, sowing the seeds of desolation and ruin in society. Wesley says of the sons and daughters that their death was a debt they owed to their own sins, which debt God may require when he pleaseth, and he could not take it in more honourable circumstances than these, that the death of a very few in the beginning of a new empire, and of their settlement in the land, might be useful to prevent the deaths of many thousands who took warning by this dreadful example, whom, if the fear of God did not, yet the love of their own and of their dear children's lives would restrain from such pernicious practices. It is very probable they were conscious of the fact, as the Jewish doctors affirm; if it be pretended that some of them were infants, the text does not say so, but only calls them sons and daughters, and considering that Achan was an old man, as is most probable because he was the fifth person from Judah, it seems most likely that the children were grown up and so capable of knowing and concealing or discovering this fact. The oxen, asses and sheep, though not capable of sin nor of punishment properly so called, yet as they were made for man's use are rightly destroyed for man's good; and being daily killed for our bodily food, it cannot seem strange to kill them for the instruction of our minds, that hereby we might learn the contagious nature of sin, which involves innocent creatures in its plagues, and how much sorer punishments are reserved for man, whose guilt, having a law given him and the excellent gift of reason and will to restrain him, must needs be unspeakably greater. By this enumeration, he adds, it appears that Achan had no colour of necessity to induce him to this fact. Of the execution Wesley says they were stoned, which was the punishment of such offenders, and not burned to death, but God would have their dead carcases burned to show his utmost detestation of such persons as break forth into sins of such public scandal and mischief; and the heap of stones was a monument of the sin and judgment here mentioned, that others might be warned by the example, and a brand of infamy. The valley of Achor is the valley of trouble, from the double trouble expressed in the sentence.

Ellicott says all were evidently destroyed together, and that for any other sin but this Achan must have suffered alone, since the children shall not be put to death for the fathers; but in this case warning had been given that the man who took of the accursed thing would be an accursed thing like it if he brought it into his house, and would make the camp of Israel accursed also, and thus Achan's whole establishment was destroyed as though it had become part of Jericho. It is not necessary to assert that the family of Achan were accomplices, he says: his cattle were not so, and yet they were destroyed; and he points to the Chronicles, where his line is not continued, and to the incidental reference that that man perished not alone in his iniquity. The severity of the punishment must be estimated by the relation of Achan's crime to the whole plan of the conquest of Canaan: if the destruction of the Canaanites was indeed the execution of the divine vengeance, it must be kept entirely clear of all baser motives, lest men should say that Jehovah gave his people licence to deal with the Canaanites as it seemed best for themselves. The punishment of Saul for taking the spoil of Amalek, and the repeated statement of the book of Esther that the Jews who stood for their lives and slew their enemies laid not their hands on the prey, are further illustrations of the same principle: the gratification of human passions may not be mingled with the execution of the vengeance of God. Of the name he says that in the Chronicles Achan himself is designated Achar, one among several examples of the alteration of a name to suit some circumstance of a person's history, comparing Bathsheba for Bathshua, Shallum for Jehoiachin and Ishbosheth for Eshbaal; and there is a double play upon the names in Hosea, where the vineyards are promised, comparing Carmi, and the valley of trouble is given for a door of hope. The valley of Achor is a pass leading from Gilgal towards the centre of the country, or as it might be represented from Jericho towards Jerusalem, that is, from the city of destruction to the city of God, and so it was to Israel in the conquest. The future state of Achan, he adds, is in the hands of the Judge who doeth judgment; no mercy to his crime on earth was possible, and it would have been injustice to all mankind. Keil says that after Joshua had once more pronounced sentence in the place of judgment, saying how hast thou troubled us and the Lord will trouble thee this day, all Israel stoned him with stones and burned them with fire; they raised over him a great heap of stones unto this day, so the Lord turned from the fierceness of his anger, and the name of that place was called the valley of Achor unto this day.

debates: Whether Achan's children died with him: Clarke argues at length from the singular and plural pronouns, the Vulgate, Septuagint, Syriac, Targum, Anglo-Saxon and De Rossi's manuscripts that Achan alone was stoned and only his goods burnt, while Ellicott holds all were evidently destroyed together and Wesley defends the deaths as a debt owed to their own sins

Whether the children were accomplices: Wesley thinks it probable they knew and concealed the theft, as the Jewish doctors affirm, and infers from Achan's descent that they were grown; Clarke finds no evidence of complicity and appeals to the law forbidding it; Ellicott says complicity need not be asserted at all, since the cattle were not accomplices and perished

What Achan's own end was: Clarke concludes that his repentance and confession were genuine and that while justice required his life mercy was extended to the salvation of his soul, whereas Ellicott says only that his future state is in the hands of the Judge who doeth judgment, no mercy to his crime on earth being possible

Whether Joshua's words at the execution were too harsh: Calvin grants the invective seems excessively harsh, as if to drive the man to frantic madness, and resolves it either as spoken for the people's instruction or as aimed at breaking a contumacy Achan had shown in complaining that his satisfaction was not accepted
outliers: Calvin's reason for executing outside the camp, that some trace of humanity should remain even in legitimate punishments
Calvin's note that circumcision, the infallible symbol of adoption, was engraved on the flesh of the sons who were nonetheless adjudged to death
Calvin's suggestion that death may have proved a medicine to them, and that if reprobate their condemnation could not be premature
Calvin's practical reason for the heap, to keep anyone from imprudently gathering particles of gold or silver on the spot
Clarke's survey of the versions, in which the Arabic alone names the children and two of De Rossi's manuscripts read him for them
Ellicott's reading of the valley as a pass from Jericho toward Jerusalem, from the city of destruction to the city of God
Gill's caution that God turning from his anger means the effects ceased, there being properly no change in God nor such passions in him as in man
